entries.title: Binance crypto exchange suspends trades over North Korea-linked hack
entries.summary: Crypto platform Binance has suspended trading following a suspected hack now linked to North Korea. The disruption has left users unable to trade on the cryptocurrency platform while the suspected breach is investigated.
entries.content:
October 30, 2026

Crypto platform Binance has suspended trading following a suspected hack now linked to North Korea. The disruption has left users unable to trade on the cryptocurrency platform while the suspected breach is investigated.

Blockchain analysts said a North Korean hacking unit was likely behind the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals for security checks and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.

US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as an elite North Korean hacking unit.

"We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said in a report published Thursday.

Why do analysts suspect North Korea?

TRM said attackers moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes. It described the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," the firm said.

Bybit lost $1.5 billion in a hack in February 2025. The FBI attributed that attack to North Korea and TraderTraitor.

Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain analysis company Chainalysis, also said the Binance attack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor.

Experts say North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities to obtain foreign currency and help fund its nuclear program despite international sanctions.

What has Binance said about the hack?

Binance did not confirm the attribution to North Korea, saying it was "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Binance said it worked to secure the affected assets and that it had located and frozen about $3 billion (€2.7 billion) so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion.

"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.

Binance said its initial investigation suggested an attacker had compromised a software infrastructure engineer's laptop, gaining access to an internal service and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The company said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked.

Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.

The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.

Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?

Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.

Edited by Sean Sinico and Karl Sexton

entries.title: Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
entries.summary: German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.
entries.content:
Middle East

Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results

October 30, 2026

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead the new government. Although the right-wing bloc including religious hardliners led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset. Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult. 

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin. but he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.

Alabali Radovan: 'Winter in Gaza will be difficult'

One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza — and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers in the West Bank and east Jerusalem on Palestinian residents: "The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end." All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.

More distanced from Netanyahu's government

Relations between Germany and Israel have long been particularly close — in part due to Germany's historical responsibility for the murder of millions of European Jews during the Nazi era. Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians. 

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after the election. So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.

CDU hoping for a centrist government

At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremist, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people — and above all, the elected politicians — will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."

The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made big gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.

However, Netanyahu’s bloc and various parties have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties. Eisenkot's bloc has not stated whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.

Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable. "The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority." The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW. "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Russia: Critical newspaper 'Novaya Gazeta' to close
entries.summary: "Novaya Gazeta," one of the last remaining independent, critical media outlets in Russia, has announced it is closing under pressure from state authorities. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, evacuations have begun in Oleshky.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Critical newspaper 'Novaya Gazeta' to close

October 30, 2026

"Novaya Gazeta," one of the last remaining independent, critical media outlets in Russia, has announced it is closing under pressure from state authorities. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, evacuations have begun in Oleshky.

The independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is shutting down and ceasing operations under pressure from state authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor.

"They've killed us," read a statement published on the newspaper's website on Friday morning.

"The Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," added editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov in a video statement. "On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave."

What is the Novaya Gazeta?

Founded in 1993 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Novaya Gazeta (Russian for "New Newspaper") was one of the few remaining critical media outlets in Russia, known for its investigations into corruption and its critical coverage of Russian politics.

It has always operated under pressure from state authorities but circumstances have deteriorated dramatically since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with the Kremlin introducing near-Soviet levels of media censorship.

The vast majority of independent journalists have been forced into exile and those who have remained in Russia have been designated "foreign agents" — a label which imposes a wide range of restrictions in everyday life including on the right to earn income from rent, interest payments or royalties from intellectual work.

A former Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief, ​Dmitry Muratov, dedicated his 2021 Nobel Peace ​Prize to six colleagues who were killed because ​of their work — including Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by the Russian military in Chechnya and was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin's birthday in October 2006.

"More than 30 years of life together with our country and its citizens will now end on the street," wrote the newspaper in its editorial, "without a basis for existence and under constant threat of repression."

The announcement of the outlet's closure comes two weeks after veteran editor-in-chief Sokolov was questioned by investigators in Moscow over "unlawful use of personal data" in connection with a criminal case against a colleague, Oleg Roldugin.

Roldugin had been detained and charged with obtaining "unlawful access to computerized information," an offence that carries a prison term of up to 10 years. No further details were given and Roldugin has pleaded not guilty.

International media rights groups have slammed the targeting of the Novaya Gazeta, with Reporters Without Borders calling on the Kremlin to "put an end to the judicial harassment" of its journalists.

Novaya Gazeta: 'The story of a country and a society being finished off'

In its editorial, the Novaya Gazeta wrote that its closure reflected the state of modern Russia under President Putin.

"This isn't just our personal story; it's the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way," it wrote.

"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated and their protection has been equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies have been de facto eliminated. Public institutions have been dismantled. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands.

"The courts have been destroyed, along with the law and the rule of law. Holding one's own convictions is now treason. But treason is when a state betrays its own Constitution. And this treason is an ongoing crime, currently unfolding before the eyes of the entire world."

Oleshky: evacuations begin amid localized truce

Meanwhile, in Ukraine, the evacuation of stranded residents from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky began on Friday as a localized US-brokered ceasefire continued to hold into a fourth day.

Captured by Russian troops early in the war in 2022, locals had endured food, water and medicine shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, residents told the AFP news agency.

The population of Oleshky has since dropped from 24,000 to about 2,000, many of whom were on Friday set to be evacuated either to Russian-controlled or Ukrainian-controlled territory.

"Evacuation and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun," said Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia while Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova posted a video showing groups of people waiting to board buses.

The local ceasefire— announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week — is the longest pause in fighting anywhere in Ukraine since the 2022 invasion. It is due to end on Sunday evening.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Brazil's new anti-gang law: Can it curb organized crime?
entries.summary: A tough stance against organized crime? One year after a massacre that left more than 130 people dead, a new law aims to crack down on drug cartels in Rio's favelas.
entries.content:
October 30, 2026

A tough stance against organized crime? One year after a massacre that left more than 130 people dead, a new law aims to crack down on drug cartels in Rio's favelas.

One year after the deadliest police operation in the history of Brazil, human rights organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) has leveled serious accusations against the country's authorities.

Contrary to legal regulations, most of the 2,500 police officers who were deployed to the "Complexo do Alemao" and "Complexo da Penha" favelas on October 28, 2025, did not wear body cameras.

In the course of "Operacao Contencao" ("Operation Containment"), police officers were expected to execute dozens of arrest warrants against members of the Comando Vermelho drug cartel that day.

The result: During hours-long firefights in the favelas, 117 alleged gang members and five police officers were killed.

Body cameras don't show the full picture

After analyzing more than 4,000 hours of video material, HRW concluded in its investigation that only around one quarter of the deployed police officers were wearing body cameras and that some were manipulated. Not a single deadly shooting was captured on camera.

"It's clear to us that a decision by the Supreme Court according to which the police in Rio must wear body cameras was violated," said HRW Brazil director Cesar Munoz.

The organization published its report in Rio de Janeiro on October 28.

Having analyzed the autopsy findings, HRW also concludes that many bodies show signs of execution, i.e. the killing of persons already incapable of fighting.

For example, 40% of those killed were shot in the head, and 75% were shot in the back. There were reasons to believe, Munoz said, that the operation "was obviously designed to be lethal."

The police operation carried out under the supervision of the state government of Rio de Janeiro shocked the country. However, there were soon calls to intensify the fight against organized crime.

Fighting drug gangs and militias

In response, the "Anti-gang Law" ("Lei Antifaccao") came into force in March 2026. It is aimed at combating criminal gangs like the PCC, a drug gang based in Sao Paulo, or the Comando Vermelho (CV), which dominates Rio.

However, militias (gangs made up of corrupt police officers and soldiers) are also to be dismantled, both criminally and economically. "The law addresses a real problem," Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety (FBSP) NGO told DW.

This was because the ability of criminal organizations to control territories, move funds and make inroads into economic activities and public institutions had expanded.

It was positive, he added, that the law extends tools for asset tracing, finance tracking, institutional cooperation and capital withdrawal to these organizations.

Another improvement, said HRW Brazil's Cesar Munoz, was closer cooperation between state security agencies. The federal police, which reports to the central government, was to play a greater role in combating gangs in the future.

In Brazil, military and civil police report to state governments. During the deadly operations in Rio de Janeiro's favelas, one year ago, command was under the authority of the state government of Rio de Janeiro — and, consequently, under the influence of local politics.

Overcrowded prisons and recruitment behind bars

On the other hand, however, the law was raising constitutional concerns, said the FBSP's Azevedo. For example, it provides for the automatic imposition of pretrial detention on suspects.

Other plans included expansion of grounds for arrest, restrictions on the easing of prison conditions — such as furloughs and the suspension of the remainder of a sentence — as well as an extension of the length of stay in prisons.

This could further exacerbate Brazil's chronic prison overcrowding. "Brazil already has one of the largest prison populations worldwide, and the law could accelerate its growth," said Azevedo.

In addition, prison overcrowding in Brazil had the perverse side effect of allowing crime syndicates such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho to recruit new members there.

"Overcrowded prisons without adequate government control facilitate recruitment and strengthening of the very criminal factions that legislation intend to combat," Azevedo concluded.

"It would be important to prevent gangs from recruiting young people and to show those who've committed crimes new prospects in life," HRW's Cesar Munoz told DW.

Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of FBSP also sees a constitutional problem in the cancellation of prison assistance — a benefit that the state paid to the prisoners' dependents.

"Its cancellation means economic punishment for those who haven't committed any crime at all, including children. This runs afoul of the constitutional principle according to which punishments must not extend beyond the convicted person," Azevedo said.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: IIHF ordered to allow Russia back into world championships
entries.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to take part in international ice hockey tournaments. The IIHF had banned Russia following the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

Russia to return to international ice hockey after CAS ruling

October 30, 2026

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to take part in international ice hockey tournaments. The IIHF had banned Russia following the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement published on Friday, the Court of Arbitration for Sport(CAS) said it had overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions, which exclude Russia from events during the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's world championships.

In the statement, the CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support security concerns cited by the IIHF in its decisions to exclude Russian teams from competition.

Specifically, it ordered the IIHF to allow Russia to participate in five upcoming tournaments, including the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany next May and the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship scheduled for November 2027 in Canada.

The first tournament affected by the ruling is the Men's World Junior Championship, which opens in Edmonton on December 26. The Women's World Championship being hosted by Denmark starting next Friday, November 6, is not mentioned in the statement.

Russia happy to be back, others less so

Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov hailed the CAS ruling, writing on the Telegram social media app that CAS had "recognized the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified."

The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling , saying it "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions."

"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."

'Political and economic consequences' for hosts Germany

Germany's ice hockey association, the DEB, also expressed disappointment at the decision. 

"Our position is unchanged: We reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments," said DEB chairman Frank Lutz, who added that the ruling had fundamentally changed things for Germany as hosts of the 2027 Men's World Championship.

"Allowing Russia to participate entails significant security-related, political, and economic consequences for us as hosts. We are now evaluating the ruling together with the IIHF and will provide information regarding the next steps."

In its statement, the IIHF also pointed to "significant practical implications for competitions already at an advanced stage of preparation," which includes the men's tournament to be hosted by Düsseldorf, Mannheim and Gelsenkirchen and for which the groups have already been drawn.

The IIHF has barred Russian teams from its tournaments since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. This meant Russia also missed this year's prestigious Olympic hockey tournaments in Milan earlier this year.

Russia and its predecessor, the Soviet Union, are one of the most successful ice hockey-playing nations, having won 27 men's World Championships, second only to Canada (28).

Friday's ruling comes with the IIHF having just elected a new president – Germany's Franz Reindl took over from Luc Tardif of France earlier this month.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age
entries.summary: West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers on October 30, 1961. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' can't live from their pensions.
entries.content:
Turkey

65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty

October 30, 2026

West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers on October 30, 1961. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' can't live from their pensions.

Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.

At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity. 

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

Some upward mobility among migrants, but discrimination a big problem

According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.

Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.

But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.

"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.

Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.

One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."

But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.

They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.

"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."

Pensions €360 lower among Turkish citizens in Germany

An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.

Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.

"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.

"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

Few chances for migrant workers to train

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.

It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.

"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."

Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.

This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.

According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).

"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.

The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.

"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism
entries.summary: From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.
entries.content:
October 30, 2026

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

A particularly iconic animal

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Germany's 'badger dog'

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

An evolving cultural icon

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

A symbol of the 'other' side Germany

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Germany news: Merz in Asia warns against weaponizing trade
entries.summary: German diplomacy in Asia takes focus this week, as Chancellor Merz wraps up a three-country Asian business tour in South Korea. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier held talks with Xi Jinping in Beijing. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz in Asia warns against weaponizing trade

Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026

German diplomacy in Asia takes focus this week, as Chancellor Merz wraps up a three-country Asian business tour in South Korea. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier held talks with Xi Jinping in Beijing. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in South Korea on the last stop of a three-country Asia tour
  • Merz calls for global trade to be strengthened and for a rules-based economic order
  • President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
  • Berlin event set to mark the 65th anniversary of West Germany and Turkey's agreement on 'guest workers'

Here are the leading headlines from and about Germany on Friday, October 30:

Skip next section Chinese President Xi lauds 'new chapter' of Germany-China ties

Chinese President Xi lauds 'new chapter' of Germany-China ties

Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.

"We both bear responsibility for the ⁠international order ​and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.

President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.

"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.

Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.

The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year. 

Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: 65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty

IN DEPTH: 65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty

On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.

Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.

Skip next section Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did

Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.

North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.

"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.

"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.

North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state." 

Skip next section German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China

German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year. 

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Skip next section Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'

Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order. 

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz said.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

Additional reporting by Nina Haase

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany seeks new head of state

IN DEPTH: Germany seeks new head of state

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Read DW's full report on who may be the next German president.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

Germany's chancellor and president were both in Asia this week, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for more robust trade ties with middle powers and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier focusing on diplomacy   during a multi-day visit to China.

On Friday, Merz spoke at a German-South Korean business conference in Seoul, while Steinmeier is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Keep reading for the latest updates from Germany.

entries.title: India news: Space agency to boost GPS alternative with new satellite
entries.summary: The Indian national space agency's mission aims to strengthen its indigenous navigation system and reduce reliance on the US-owned GPS. Meanwhile, Rahul Gandhi renewed his call for more election protests. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Space agency to boost GPS alternative with new satellite

Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026

The Indian national space agency's mission aims to strengthen its indigenous navigation system and reduce reliance on the US-owned GPS. Meanwhile, Rahul Gandhi renewed his call for more election protests. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The NVS-03 satellite will be carried into orbit by the GSLV-F18 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota
  • It aims to boost NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to the US Global Positioning System (GPS) system
  • Opposition leader Gandhi renews call for November 1 rally 'to save democracy'

Here are the top headlines from India on Friday, October 30:

Skip next section Six feared dead in helicopter crash in Uttarakhand

Six feared dead in helicopter crash in Uttarakhand

Six people were feared dead ⁠in the Indian Himalayan state of Uttarakhand on Friday following a ‌helicopter ⁠crash suspected to have been caused by bad weather.

The helicopter ​was ‌reportedly carrying five passengers ‌and ​a pilot from Badrinath, a prominent Hindu pilgrimage destination in the ‌mountains, to the city of Dehradun, according to news agency ANI.

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said his office ​had received information about a helicopter crashing near a village in the ⁠Joshimath ​area.

Dhami said rescue operations were being carried out by the district ​administration, disaster management ‌teams and army personnel in the region.

Skip next section Opposition leader Gandhi urges supporters to rally 'to save democracy'

Opposition leader Gandhi urges supporters to rally 'to save democracy'

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Friday renewed his call for supporters of his Congress Party and other opposition groups to demonstrate this weekend at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi, a large open space usually serving as a venue for religious festivals. 

Gandhi and other senior opposition figures are seeking to capitalize on growing public discontent over alleged voter roll irregularities.

Gandhi encouraged people to turn out to protest on Sunday, despite recent clampdowns by police.

"This is not a march for any one political party, it's a march for the soul of India," Gandhi said.

"If you feel that India is under attack, you are under attack, your expression, your ideas, your way of thinking is under attack, come and join us."

Recent protests against alleged electoral fraud in India have seen protesters and police clash, with several protest leaders detained.

The largely youth- and student-led demonstrations have grown into one of the most serious challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government in years.

But Gandhi said: "Don't worry about the police ... the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics."

Skip next section Uttar Pradesh MLC election result sends warning to BJP from Samajwadi Party

Uttar Pradesh MLC election result sends warning to BJP from Samajwadi Party

The Legislative Council elections results declared on Thursday in the northern Uttar Pradesh state has thrust the Samajwadi Party (SP) back in the limelight against the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ahead of the state elections next year.

SP strengthened its position in Uttar Pradesh's Legislative Council after winning five of the 11 seats contested.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP retained its overall tally of six seats.

SP president Akhilesh Yadav described the results as a rejection of the BJP's policies on education, teachers and students.

"None of our candidates has actually lost, they just could not win in the face of the BJP’s manipulation," Yadav said, according to The Indian Express newspaper, without providing evidence.

Skip next section West Bengal, Assam on flood alert after glacial lake outburst in Bhutan

West Bengal, Assam on flood alert after glacial lake outburst in Bhutan

Several districts in West Bengal, along with parts of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, were placed on flood alert on Friday, media reports said.

The flood, triggered by a glacial lake burst at Sintaphu Lake in neighboring Bhutan, swept away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu natural hot springs in the Himalayan kingdom.

Indian authorities have stepped up monitoring along the Sankosh River, which flows from Bhutan through West Bengal and into Assam. Communities along the Brahmaputra River in Assam and Arunachal Pradesh have also been alerted over possible flooding.

In Bhutan, no casualties have been reported, state broadcaster BBS said.

According to Bhutanese media reports, two Bailey bridges, built in portable, pre-fabricated sections, may have been washed away, as well as a part of the road leading to Laya village, where the hot springs are located, had also been washed away.

Skip next section India to launch new satellite to reduce reliance on US-owned GPS

India to launch new satellite to reduce reliance on US-owned GPS

India's space agency is set to launch a navigation satellite on Friday night to strengthen the country's indigenous alternative to GPS.

According to Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) the NVS-03 is "intended to augment the NavIC constellation and support continuity of navigation services."

The NVS-03 satellite, the third in ISRO's next-generation navigation series, will be carried into orbit by the GSLV-F18 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota at 11:51 p.m. (1821 GMT) on Friday.

According to ISRO, the satellite features an indigenous atomic clock alongside imported clocks, and adds the L1 signal to the existing L5 and S-band signals. It is designed to provide navigation coverage across India and up to 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) beyond its borders.

NavIC is seen as an alternative to the Global Positioning System (GPS) system owned by the United States government.

It was developed to reduce India's dependence on foreign navigation systems, however, according to the Hindustan Times newspaper, the program has faced repeated setbacks, including failing atomic clocks and satellite launch and deployment problems.

Last month, India had launched of its EOS-05 Earth observation satellite, its first ever imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the top updates from across India.

All eyes will be on the skies today as India prepares to launch a navigation satellite to strengthen its indigenous alternative to GPS, reducing the country's reliance on the US government-owned system.

Meanwhile, the results of the Legislative Council elections in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh serve as a warning from the Samajwadi Party to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ahead of the 2027 state elections.

Elsewhere, the states of Assam and West Bengal are on flood alert after a glacier burst in Bhutan.

For all this and more, follow our blog.

entries.title: Israeli election: Netanyahu, main rival fall short of majority after all votes counted
entries.summary: With all the votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc finished ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc. But tough coalition talks loom as neither grouping won a majority. DW has more.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Majority remains elusive after final count

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 30, 2026

With all the votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc finished ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc. But tough coalition talks loom as neither grouping won a majority. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has been closed. Thank you for reading.

Below is a roundup of the main developments from the Israeli election:

  • Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
  • The final vote count showed Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc finished with 53 seats
  • The anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, claimed 48 seats
  • At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
  • As neither party won an outright majority, difficult coalition talks are expected in the weeks ahead

Skip next section WATCH: How do Gazans feel about the coalition stalemate in Israel?

WATCH: How do Gazans feel about the coalition stalemate in Israel?

Gazans weigh in on the current coalition stalemate after Israel went to the polls on October 27 with neither major bloc reaching a governing majority. The coalition that emerges will largely determine whether Israeli policy in Gaza continues on its current course.

Skip next section WATCH: How will Arab party gains impact coalition talks?

WATCH: How will Arab party gains impact coalition talks?

Arab parties have made a historic breakthrough in Israel's election, achieving their strongest showing in years. Their success could give Arab lawmakers unprecedented influence over coalition negotiations.

But it's unclear whether those gains will translate into real political power.

Skip next section Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins

Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins

Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.

On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.

However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.

The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.

Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.

He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.

It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.

Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.

Skip next section Final count released

Final count released

The final count of ballots from Tuesday's vote has been released by Israel's Central Election Committee.

Netanyahu's bloc with a total of 53 seats

  • Likud - 27
  • UTJ - 7
  • Otzma Yehudit - 7
  • Shas - 6
  • RZP - 6

Eisenkot's bloc with a total of 48 seats

  • Yashar - 21
  • B'Yachad - 12
  • The Democrats - 8
  • Yisrael Beytenu - 7

The Arab Israeli parties with a total of 19 seats

  • Joint List - 11
  • Ra'am - 8

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Authorities dispute Netanyahu's fraud claims

IN DEPTH: Authorities dispute Netanyahu's fraud claims

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims. 

Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative" nor "informative."

A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.

Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here. 

Skip next section Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon

Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon

With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.

  • Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
  • Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
  • Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
  • Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
  • Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
  • Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
  • Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
  • The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
  • Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
  • "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.

Skip next section Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end

With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.

That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.

The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.

Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.

The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.

Skip next section Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.

Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.

According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.

This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.

The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.

Skip next section UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law. 

"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.

"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."

Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.

He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."

Skip next section 'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.

"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."

Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.

"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.

Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.

Skip next section WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.

Some small positives may be possible though.

Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.

Skip next section GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

Skip next section Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.

These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.

This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.

Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.

Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.

If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.

Skip next section President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.

"I will receive  the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions." 

Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.

"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
